L378@P11: Harappa Phase Carved Seals
L379@P11: Only two seals, both incomplete, have been recovered from the lowest levels of the Harappa
L380@P11: Phase (Period 3A). One example (H-1688) is a broken steatite seal from street deposits on
L381@P11: Mound E, dating to ca. 2600 Be. (Kenoyer 1991; Dales, Kenoyer et al. 1991, fig. 13.44e). The
L382@P11: style of carving is bold and angular, consisting of a single sign above the rump of a bovine,
L383@P11: which, to judge by comparison with a complete seal from the site of Farmana in Haryana,
L384@P11: might be a water buffalo (Shinde et al. 2008: 104, fig. 107). The deeply carved V-shaped sign
L385@P11: or symbol has not been found on any later seal, but a rounder and more symmetrical form does
L386@P11: occur on molded tablets. The animals carved on later seals also are more naturalistic with
L387@P11: smooth contours that reflect the actual muscles ofthe animal.
L388@P11: The second Period 3A seal fragment from Harappa (H-1689) comes from a deposit on the
L389@P11: western edge of Mound E that was found to contain both Early Harappan and Harappan pottery. This seal has an elephant motifwith naturalistic lines and may represent the development
L390@P11: of seal carving styles at the end of Period 3A or the beginning of Period 3B. Further welldated examples are needed to clarify the earliest style of seal carving, but these two seal fragments from Harappa, and the examples from Farmana, suggest that styles of carving seals
L391@P11: evolved over time and that some ofthe signs also changed over time.
L392@P11: Our excavations have recovered unfinished and finished seals from contexts some of
L393@P11: which can be accurately dated and associated with specific activity areas at Harappa. Unfinished seals have been recovered from across the site, and through detailed comparisons, it
L394@P11: may be possible to identify specific workshop styles and changes in carving techniques. One
L395@P11: of the unfinished unicorn seals (H-1683), a fragment of which was found on the northeastern
L396@P11: slope of Mound E, has such a distinctive style of carving used for the ritual stand - as well as
L397@P11: for the unicorn's collar, ear, and horn - that it should be readily identifiable on finished seals.
L398@P11: Indeed, a comparable carving style is seen on a finished unicorn seal (H-1682) from a Period
L399@P11: 3B context in a nearby trench on the eastern edge of Mound E some distance from where the
L400@P11: unfinished seal was found.
L401@P11: Silicone impressions have been taken of all seals with well-preserved surfaces, and finegrained molds from these can be used to make high-resolution photographs with a scanning
L402@P11: electron microscope (Kenoyer 1997; 2003). This technique provides the means to identify distinctive features of tool marks and cutting angles, which then can be compared between seals.
L403@P11: Such a process can lead to the definition of tool types and even to identification of specific
L404@P11-12: tools and special features of carving technique, all of which can assist us to understand theliv J MARK KENOYER & RICHARD H. MEADOW
L405@P12: nature, development and even the organization ofseal-carving traditions. Already we can suggest, based on the recovery of unfinished seals with only the animal motif present, that this
L406@P12: part ofthe seal was carved first, followed by the script. Going further, using the evidence provided by detailed characterizations of carving style and technique, it may be possible to determine if one artisan carved animal motifs while another artisan specialized in carving the script.
L407@P12: In the end, it may also be possible to define specific workshops and even individual artisans. lO
L408@P12: One rare example of a seal without any animal motif(H-1692) was recovered in a dustbin
L409@P12: outside of a house at the northeastern edge of Mound E. The house associated with this structure can be dated to Period 3B, and this seal may represent an early example of what was to
L410@P12: become the long rectangular seal with script (e.g. H-1704 to H-1715) that became quite common in subsequent Period 3C. This early example, however, is only slightly longer than it is
L411@P12: wide and has the grooved boss typical of seals with animal motifs. Examples of similar types
L412@P12: of seals have been reported from Mohenjo-daro (CISI 1, p. 78: M-313, M-316, M-315) and
L413@P12: Lothal (CISI 1, p. 251: L-56, L-58, L-59), but for those sites the context and dating of such
L414@P12: seals are not well understood.
L415@P12: Chronological Aspects of Boss Types
L416@P12: One important feature of seals that is worth further study is variation in styles of perforated
L417@P12: bosses used to string or hold seals. Based on the stratigraphic and chronological contexts of
L418@P12: seals found from Harappa, there appears to be significant changes in the types of boss used
L419@P12: during different periods and on different types ofseals. In this introductory section, we present
L420@P12: a summary ofthe major types and provide some comparative examples from other sites. 11
L421@P12: So far no complete button seals have been found from the Ravi phase (Period 1), but the
L422@P12: carved bone button seal fragment (H-1521) has a hole in the center like button seals found
L423@P12: from the Chalcolithic deposits of Mehrgarh (CISI 2, p. 403: Mr-l0 to Mr-14) and the carved
L424@P12: ivory button seal from Rahman-dheri (CISI 2, p. 352: Rhd-l).
L425@P12: Two types of attachment devices have been found on the button seals from the Kat Diji
L426@P12: Phase (Period 2) levels. Four ofthe button seals have evidence for a raised knob or boss on the
L427@P12: back, but one circular button seal (Kenoyer & Meadow 2008: 127, fig. 4.3 - illustrated above
L428@P12: in fig. 2) has two parallel holes through the body of the disc and no knob on the back. Of the
L429@P12: seals with evidence for a boss, two examples have a raised circular knob with a flat end and
L430@P12: the perforation passing laterally through the knob (this volume: H-1535, H-1536). As noted
L431@P12: above, similar seals have been reported for sites such as Tarakai Qila, Kalibangan, Kunal, and
L432@P12: Rahman-dheri. Also as noted previously, an unfinished geometric seal (H-1534), found in a
L433@P12: mixed context but attributed to Period 2, has what appears to be a repaired knob where a portion may have cracked off the back and an attempt made to prepare an off-center perforated
L434@P12: knob. Traces of a similar type of knob fragment are seen on the back of the unfinished elephant seal that comes from a sealed context of Period 2 (H-1533 and Kenoyer & Meadow
L435@P12: 2008: 127, fig. 4.8).

L440@P13: During Harappa Phase Periods 3A and 3B, the most common form of boss for most seal
L441@P13: types is the circular dome-shaped boss with a single central groove. Rarely this type of boss
L442@P13: has a double groove, as at the site of Gola Dhoro (Bagasara), Gujarat (Bhan et al. 2005). The
L443@P13: perforation is generally oriented horizontally in the same direction as the script and animal
L444@P13: motif. The drilling for the perforation is done from both sides and angled down so that the hole
L445@P13: meets deep inside the seal body rather than at the level of the boss itself. This drilling technique was necessary to avoid weakening the small area where the boss joins the seal body.
L446@P13: Nevertheless, a common form ofseal breakage is detachment ofthe boss because of the weak
L447@P13: structure ofsteatite itself. 12
L448@P13: Another form of boss found during Harappa Phase Periods 3B and 3C is usually on steatite seals with geometric designs such as circle and dot motifs (H-1700, H-1702). The boss is a
L449@P13: simple raised square with a flat or convex surface and a transverse perforation. Similar types
L450@P13: of bosses are found on a variety offaience button seals also dated to Periods 3B/C and 3C.
L451@P13: During the final phase of the Harappan occupation (Period 3C) the single grooved boss
L452@P13: continues to be used on square seals. On the long rectangular seals, however, there is no separate knob, with the perforation being drilled transversely through the sides of the central and
L453@P13: thickest part ofthe seal. 13 There are a few exceptions to this pattern and two ofthe long rectangular seals recovered in earlier excavations from Harappa have a grooved knob or boss on the
L454@P13: back (CISII, p. 203: H-161, H-162).
L455@P13: Another form of boss that appears in period 3C is a domed or convex form found on
L456@P13: square geometric seals. The domed back is usually decorated with concentric circles or floral
L457@P13: motifs. Two seals of this type were found in mixed contexts and erroneously attributed to
L458@P13: Period 2 in earlier publications (Kenoyer & Meadow 2008: 127, figs. 4.4 and 4.5 = H-2588 in
L459@P13: fig. 2.1 above and H-1537). Recent analysis of the carving technique and the nature of the
L460@P13: glazed surface suggest that these seals do not date to Period 2, but should be associated with
L461@P13: Period 3C. This type of boss has not been discovered in the Early Harappan (Harappa Period
L462@P13: 2) levels at any other site in the greater Indus region. This style of carving on the domed boss
L463@P13: is common on circular seals associated with the Persian Gulfregion. The circular seal from the
L464@P13: area of Lothal with four circle and dot motifs on its face, however, has a triple incised line
L465@P13: across its domed boss (CISI I, p. 268: L-123).
L466@P13: There is one example from Harappa of a circular button seal (H-1703) with a raised circular boss with a flat top, but this seal was found in surface deposits and thus its chronological
L467@P13: placement cannot be determined. It is possible that it dates to the Late Harappan or postHarappan period based on broadly similar geometric button seals from the site ofChanhu-daro
L468@P13: during the Jhukar or Late Harappan period (Mackay 1943, PI. XLIX) and from Pirak dating to
L469@P13: the post-Harappan period (Jarrige, Santoni & Enault 1979; CISI 2, p. 381: Pk-15 to Pk-17).
L470@P13: 12 Ifthis happened while a seal was hanging on a cord worn at the waist or neck, the seal could easily have been
L471@P13: lost in the street as a person was traveling through the city. While a number ofseals are found broken into two or
L472@P13: more pieces in dumps and in the streets, other inscribed pieces from similar contexts are complete. Althongh it is
L473@P13: possible to snggest that some devices may have been broken intentionally in order to cancel them out and prevent

L479@P14: Conclusions
L480@P14: When both seal carving styles and boss types are considered together, there is good evidence
L481@P14: for an evolution in seal forms over time. Whether there were parallel changes in the script
L482@P14: needs to be investigated in detail. In the past, studies ofthe Indus script have lumped all ofthe
L483@P14: best-preserved seal inscriptions together and used this combined assemblage as the basis for a
L484@P14: study ofthe script. Based on the discoveries at Harappa, it is now possible for that site at least
L485@P14: to separate out different chronological periods ofseal production and to compare seal inscriptions with those found on other types of objects such as incised and molded tablets and pottery, which together greatly outnumber the seals and seal impressions recovered from the site.
L486@P14: The use ofIndus signs on distinctive types of objects as well as upon ornaments and pottery indicates common cultural practice at sites ofthe Indus Civilization. This shared practice
L487@P14: may be a reflection of or have played a role in the integration of populations within and between urban centers as well as with communities spread out across rural areas, along trade
L488@P14: routes, and in resource areas. Especially as new excavations produce stratigraphically controlled and well-dated inscribed pieces, it becomes both possible and increasingly important
L489@P14: that the script and accompanying iconography be subjected to rigorous analysis at the site,
L490@P14: regional, and cross-regional levels to investigate trends of change through time and variability
L491@P14: across space. When such studies have been carried out, assumptions about the uniformity of
L492@P14: the signing system (Parpola 1994) probably will need to be revised. Even though these new
L493@P14: discoveries will not lead to a decipherment of the Indus script, any new patterns that can be
L494@P14: discerned at Harappa and at other sites where close stratigraphic and spatial documentation has
L495@P14: been possible, will help us to better interpret the role ofthe script in the Indus world.
L496@P14: In our opinion, too much scholarly (and lay) emphasis has been placed on the unattainable
L497@P14: goal of deciphennent of the Indus script and not enough on treating seals, tablets, and other
L498@P14: inscribed materials as archaeological fmds that went through processes of materials selection,
L499@P14: production, use, and discard. Choices were being made throughout the birth, life, and death of
L500@P14: inscribed objects, choices that are encoded in the objects themselves or in the archaeological
L501@P14: contexts from which they have been recovered. We have the knowledge and techniques available to identifY and decode some of these choices through the study of individual and patterned activities. That is where our focus should lie. The volumes ofthe Corpus ofIndus Seals
L502@P14: and Inscriptions are a resource that can help this to happen.
